You need to ignore everything below the headline and then read the headline as "Puppies are taking the Hugos back just in time."

The author fails to mention how the books that got nominated are somehow wrecking the Hugo awards.

From http://www.thehugoawards.org/hugo-history/2015-hugo-awards:

Best Novel (1827 nominating ballots, 587 entries, range 212-387):

  • Ancillary Sword, Ann Leckie (Orbit US/Orbit UK)
  • The Dark Between the Stars, Kevin J. Anderson (Tor Books)
  • The Goblin Emperor, Katherine Addison (Sarah Monette) (Tor Books)
  • Skin Game, Jim Butcher (Orbit UK/Roc Books)
  • The Three Body Problem, Cixin Liu, Ken Liu translator (Tor Books)

As someone who's not familiar with these pieces of fiction, can anyone show me how these books are an indication of a right-wing agenda?

The author of that article states that "Anne Leckie’s smart gender-deconstruction of space opera Ancillary Justice" was not accepted favorably by "the Puppies", in the past, yet Ann Leckie's Ancillary Sword has been nominated this year, the same year he says that right-wingers have taken over nominations. Does Ancillary Sword have a right-wing slant whereas Ancillary Justice was perfectly objective in it's fiction (I'm not sure that's even a sensible phrase)?

And by saying the nominations have been hijacked and that "The truth is that this year’s Hugo awards are wrecked.", isn't the author of the article stating that the authors of those books did not get nominated based on merit? I'd say that's some pretty bold asshattery right there. If the people who care enough about science fiction make their voices heard, and you don't like their voice, then maybe you don't get to define what science fiction should be.

The author concludes with "Locking out women writers, writers of colour, gay and trans writers does a violence to the heart of the genre. If the Puppies win, nobody wins."

So are Ann Leckie and Cixin Liu white males? The nominations for Best Novel alone removes this last and key claim of any merit. People aren't being locked out because of color or race. As for transgender or sexual orientation, how would anyone even guess that from an author's name? Why does the author even mention that? Do readers really try to trace down the 'true' gender or sexual preference of every author just to make sure they're not reading anyone who's transgender or gay? Seriously, critical analysis of this article yields a conclusion that's it's a load of horseshit or the author doesn't know the first thing about writing a persuasive argument. I'm leaning toward both of those possibilities being true.

As my knowledge currently stands, I'd say that it's likely that SF purists are preventing others with political agendas from skewing nominations.

Dawkins is a scientist. But he tells people how they should live their lives. Sure sure there are times when it is appropriate to do this. We should be reminded that washing your hands is good, or that stem cell therapy could cure a lot of things, or that there is a difference between gmos and monsanto.
Dawkins however comes from a particular brand of scientist who acts more like a priest and tells people quite assuredly what is MORALLY right/wrong.

"he responded to another user who said she would be faced with "a real ethical dilemma" if she became pregnant with a baby with Down's syndrome.

Dawkins tweeted: "Abort it and try again. It would be immoral to bring it into the world if you have the choice.""

Now, I have a couple issues with this. First off, how the FUCK are we defining morality here? ""If your morality is based, as mine is, on a desire to increase the sum of happiness and reduce suffering, the decision to deliberately give birth to a Down's baby, when you have the choice to abort it early in the pregnancy, might actually be immoral from the point of view of the child's own welfare."" Now, I've met a lot of people with downs, some of them more inept than others. But all of them were pretty happy. If you asked any of them whether or not they would WANT to be alive I'm pretty sure of what their answer would be. In suggesting it is immoral to knowingly have a kid with downs there is an indicated assumption that life's value is measured in contribution. My own opinion on the matter of this ..... morality to being alive.... is that wanting to be alive is enough to justify your capacity for life. I'm not a eugenicist, I don't think life would necessarily be better or worse without all the cripples, it would just be life. Drug addicts can require far more care than someone with downs. My other big qualm with this is that ~90% of people already abort if the know their kid has downs- people don't want to put up with that shit.

So, you have this situation where an almost universally respected scientist- one of the most respected minds of our age mind you- taking a very brave and vulnerable minority of people who make the choice to have a kid with downs, and calling it immoral. This is not what scientists are for. Scientists are meant to investigate reality, and to some degree pass judgement on how we should live within that reality. But appraising morality is really not science's job- if anything, science tells us that morality is an abstraction/perversion of our framework for how we perceive our own behavior in order to function better socially/politically. Essentially, morality is an invention that we cannot do with out (as far as I can tell anyway) and kind of have to constantly watch and maintain in order to cooperate among each other as best as possible. Scientific process is not necessarily sufficient in itself to do this. Using your personal beliefs (especially if that belief is scientific and grounded in observations of reality) to rationalize and make absolutes about something as abstract and "non"-real but important as morality is a really whack thing to do- and in my opinion is the job of bad priests/missionaries/something.

Canada prime minister Stephen Harper set to call October election

Canada’s prime minister, Stephen Harper, is poised to call a parliamentary election for October 19, kicking off a marathon 11-week campaign likely to focus on a stubbornly sluggish economy and his decade in power.

Polls indicate that Harper’s right-of-center Conservative party, which has been in office since 2006, could lose its majority in the House of Commons.

That would leave Harper at the mercy of the two main centre-left opposition parties, who could unite to bring him down. Minority governments in Canada rarely last more than 18 months.
